To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the only restrictions imposed on community excess demand systems by microeconomic theory are Walras' Law and the absence of excess demand for all goods at the initial prices.

(1) if the economy contains only one commodity, the excess demand functions are homothetic; (2) if the economy has two commodities, the excess demand function is homothetic; and (3) if the economy consists of three or more commodities, there are no additional restrictions on the excess demand function.

(a) if the economy contains at most as many commodities as consumers, then the only restriction imposed on the community excess demand functions by microeconomic theory is Walras' Law; (b) if the preferences of consumers are homothetic, then the same result holds, even though the distribution of initial wealth may be any set of independent points fixed in advance except that it may be scaled by a common factor.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of whether there are any restrictions on the behavior of an economic system which can be imposed by the assumption of homothetic preferences and which are not implied by the weaker assumption that the system is in equilibrium.
the question: What can be deduced about the structure of community excess demand functions in a pure exchange economy, if one knows that the preferences of the individual consumers are homothetic?
the problem of determining the restrictions that microeconomic theory places on the aggregate excess demand functions of an economy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the homotheticity of preferences imposes no restrictions on community excess demand systems, except that they be homogenetic, i.e., satisfy Walras' Law.
microeconomic theory is silent on community excess demand except for the case in which all the consumers have identical preferences.
microeconomic theory places almost no restriction on a community excess demand function, even when it is required to be homogeneous of degree zero, if the economy is large enough.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the microeconomic theory of consumer behavior is almost empty if we assume homotheticity and the absence of aggregate excess demand.
the theory of consumer choice is almost irrelevant to the theory of community excess demand functions.

if we are willing to assume that the consumers are identical except for a scaling of their endowments, then the only restriction imposed by microeconomic theory on the community excess demand functions is Walras' Law.
The main takeaway from our work is that
homothetic preferences impose very weak restrictions on the structure of excess demand functions.
the standard assumptions of microeconomic theory impose very little structure on community excess demand.
, if we want to use microeconomics to impose meaningful restrictions on the behavior of the community, we should not restrict ourselves to a priori assumptions on the individual's preferences.
